claim: Reproducibility is a central tenant of research.
source: Reproducibility is a central tenant of research.
evidence: This is a foundational statement presented as established knowledge in the research community.

claim: Reproducing previously published studies helps to discern discoveries from false leads.
source: Reproducing previously published studies helps us to discern discoveries from false leads.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific understanding about the purpose of reproducibility.

claim: The lexicon around reproducibility studies is diverse and poorly defined.
source: The lexicon around reproducibility studies is diverse and poorly defined (Goodman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Goodman et al., 2016.

claim: Most scientific studies are never formally reproduced.
source: Most scientific studies are never formally reproduced and some disciplines have lower rates of reproducibility attempts than others.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge in the field and is supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Some disciplines have lower rates of reproducibility attempts than others.
source: Most scientific studies are never formally reproduced and some disciplines have lower rates of reproducibility attempts than others.
evidence: This is supported by the example provided about education research and general knowledge in the field.

claim: In education research, only 0.13% (221 out of 164,589) of published articles in the discipline's top 100 journals described an independent reproducibility study in an analysis published in 2014.
source: For example, in education research, an analysis published in 2014 of all publications in the discipline's top 100 journals found that only 0.13% (221 out of 164,589) of the published articles described an independent reproducibility study (Makel and Plucker, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Makel and Plucker, 2014.

claim: There is rising concern about the reproducibility of research.
source: There is rising concern about the reproducibility of research and increasing interest in enhancing research transparency (e.g. Buck, 2015; Munafò et al., 2017; Collins and Tabak, 2014; Begley and Ioannidis, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations indicating concern in the literature.

claim: There is increasing interest in enhancing research transparency.
source: There is rising concern about the reproducibility of research and increasing interest in enhancing research transparency (e.g. Buck, 2015; Munafò et al., 2017; Collins and Tabak, 2014; Begley and Ioannidis, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A project estimating the reproducibility of 100 psychology studies published in three leading journals found that just 36% had statistically significant results, compared to 97% of the original studies.
source: For example, a project estimating the reproducibility of 100 psychology studies published in three leading journals found that just 36% had statistically significant results, compared to 97% of the original studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Open Science Collaboration, 2015 study.

claim: Just 47% of the psychology studies had effect sizes that were within the bounds of the 95% confidence interval of the original study.
source: Just 47% of the studies had effect sizes that were within the bounds of the 95% confidence interval of the original study (Open Science Collaboration, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Open Science Collaboration, 2015.

claim: A large-scale study attempting to reproduce 67 economics papers was only able to reproduce 22 (33%) of these.
source: Estimates of reproducibility in economics are similarly modest or low: a large-scale study attempting to reproduce 67 papers was only able to reproduce 22 (33%) of these (Chang and Li, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chang and Li, 2015.

claim: When teams attempting to reproduce research involved one of the original study authors as a co-author on the project, rates of reproducibility increased.
source: This same study showed that when teams attempting to reproduce research involved one of the original study authors as a co-author on the project, rates of reproducibility increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the Chang and Li, 2015 study mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: Detailed familiarity with the original study method may increase the likelihood of reproducing the research findings.
source: This may suggest that detailed familiarity with the original study method increases the likelihood of reproducing the research findings.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding about author involvement increasing reproducibility rates.

claim: A cancer biology reproducibility project launched in 2013 found that most of the selected studies could not even be attempted to be reproduced.
source: A cancer biology reproducibility project launched in 2013 to independently reproduce several high-profile papers has produced rather sobering results a decade later. Most of the selected studies could not even be attempted to be reproduced (e.g. it was not clear what had been done originally) and among those that an attempt to reproduce was made, most did not seem to produce consistent results (although the exact reproducibility rate depends on the definition of reproducibility) and the effect of the reproduced studies was only 15% of the original effect (Errington et al., 2021a; Kane and Kimmelman, 2021; Errington et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Errington et al., 2021a; Kane and Kimmelman, 2021; Errington et al., 2021b.

claim: Among cancer biology studies that an attempt to reproduce was made, most did not seem to produce consistent results.
source: A cancer biology reproducibility project launched in 2013 to independently reproduce several high-profile papers has produced rather sobering results a decade later. Most of the selected studies could not even be attempted to be reproduced (e.g. it was not clear what had been done originally) and among those that an attempt to reproduce was made, most did not seem to produce consistent results (although the exact reproducibility rate depends on the definition of reproducibility) and the effect of the reproduced studies was only 15% of the original effect (Errington et al., 2021a; Kane and Kimmelman, 2021; Errington et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Errington et al., 2021a; Kane and Kimmelman, 2021; Errington et al., 2021b.

claim: The effect of the reproduced cancer biology studies was only 15% of the original effect.
source: A cancer biology reproducibility project launched in 2013 to independently reproduce several high-profile papers has produced rather sobering results a decade later. Most of the selected studies could not even be attempted to be reproduced (e.g. it was not clear what had been done originally) and among those that an attempt to reproduce was made, most did not seem to produce consistent results (although the exact reproducibility rate depends on the definition of reproducibility) and the effect of the reproduced studies was only 15% of the original effect (Errington et al., 2021a; Kane and Kimmelman, 2021; Errington et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Errington et al., 2021a; Kane and Kimmelman, 2021; Errington et al., 2021b.
